newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain urged to sue China over HK treaty "breach".
newsitem.headline: Britain urged to sue China over HK treaty "breach".

text.p: Hong Kong pro-democracy leader Martin Lee urged Britain on Thursday to sue Beijing for what he called breaches of the Sino-British treaty on the colony's imminent return to China.
Lee, on a London visit, said on Hong Kong radio that Britain should file a legal suit at the World Court which rules on disputes between states.

With 33 days until an historic changeover ending 156 years of colonial rule, the territory's democrats are fretting about future leader Tung Chee-hwa's plans to curb civil liberties and revamp a British-style electoral system.
China and Britain meanwhile spent the day locked in diplomatic horse-trading over London's future role in Hong Kong.
Beijing's anointed future leader Tung, who celebrated his 60th birthday on Thursday, will succeed departing governor Chris Patten and looks set to scrap his democratic reforms.
Lee met new British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook in London on Wednesday and urged Blair to attend the transition ceremonies.
"I strongly urged Prime Minister Blair to attend the handover ceremony on June 30 in Hong Kong to show concern for the future of Hong Kong's six million people," Lee said.
Hong Kong's democracy lobby is refusing to cooperate with a shadow Provisional Chamber that China will install on July 1, casting an elected legislature out of office.
"I told him (Foreign Secretary Cook) that the Provisional Legislature was clearly in breach of the Sino-British Joint Declaration," Lee said.
The 1984 Joint Declaration committed Britain to returning its colony to China and tied Beijing to retaining Hong Kong's capitalist lifestyle and freedoms intact for 50 years.

Lee wants the British to take the case to the United Nations International Court of Justice in The Hague. He acknowleged China would probably exercise its veto but argues at least Britain would have focused world attention on the issue.

British and Chinese negotiators entered the second day of a final round of tense diplomatic haggling before the handover. Sources close to the talks said they were deadlocked in dispute over Britain's future role in Hong Kong.

Also on the agenda at the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), headed by ambassadors from the two countries, were discussions of the final details of the handover ceremonies and the transfer of Hong Kong government archives and assets to the post-colonial administration.

China's chief negotiator Zhao Jihua told reporters the JLG, which will serve until 2000, will be just a liaison body after the handover, and suggested that Britain should focus less on the post-change period and more on unresolved handover problems.
But British team leader Hugh Davies the JLG would continue to monitor China's implementation of the Joint Declaration well beyond the change of flag at midnight June 30.

A midnight extravaganza, attended by 4,000 VIPs including Chinese and British leaders, will bid farewell to the colonial era with a military pageant, a solemn flag raising ceremony and a sky full of fireworks.
The Democratic Party, which Lee heads, has said key leaders would attend the celebrations but rank and file members planned to stage a peaceful demonstration in the Legislative Council chamber.
Davies said departing governor Patten would play a low-key role at the ceremonies.
His democratic reforms so angered China that it immediately drew up a blueprint for the provisional legislature and ordered the scrapping of Patten's democratic reforms.
"We don't expect the Governor to deliver the speech at the ceremony. We expect the principal participant on each side will deliver a speech," Davies said.
"We, as you know, have already announced our principal participant will be the Prince of Wales."
Diplomats and government officials say they expect President Jiang Zemin to represent China.
